extraction.name: Vibravox
extraction.description: A dataset of French speech captured with five body-conduction audio sensors and a reference airborne microphone, including speech samples and physiological sounds from 188 participants under different acoustic conditions, with recording-condition annotations and linguistic transcriptions.
extraction.creator: Julien Hauret, Malo Olivier, Thomas Joubaud, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poiree, Veronique Zimpfer, and Eric Bavu
extraction.citeAs: Hauret, Julien, Malo Olivier, Thomas Joubaud, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poirée, Véronique Zimpfer, and Éric Bavu. "Vibravox: A Dataset of French Speech Captured with Body-conduction Audio Sensors." Submitted to Elsevier Speech Communication, August 20, 2024; revision submitted March 29, 2025. arXiv:2407.11828v4.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Participants were recorded with six sensors simultaneously following a four-step protocol: reading French Wikipedia sentences in quiet conditions, remaining silent in noisy conditions, remaining silent in clean conditions, and reading in noisy conditions created with a 3D spatializer.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Some recordings were excluded due to mispronunciations, sensor shifts, sensor malfunctions, or microphones left unequipped; 188 of 200 participants and 28,471 of 30,568 sentences were retained after filtering.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consist of simultaneous 6-channel audio recordings from five body-conduction sensors and one airborne headset microphone, plus French Wikipedia text and ambient noise from AudioSet and in-house ambisonic recordings.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Text was filtered and normalized; phonetic transcriptions were generated automatically and corrected manually for some words. Audio underwent a 20 Hz high-pass filter, automatic post-processing filters based on phoneme error rate and SNR, speaker-based train/validation/test splitting, VAD timestamp extension by 0.6 seconds, and 15 ms trimming when boundaries were exceeded.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The dataset includes recording-condition annotations and linguistic transcriptions. Phonetic transcriptions were generated from normalized text using the CoML lab phonemizer, with manual phonetic transcription for unrecognized words.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The authors filtered samples using phoneme error rate and signal-level criteria to ensure correct pronunciation and high-quality labels for the speech-to-phonemes task.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: CoML lab phonemizer; whisper-timestamped model based on Whisper
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to support progress in body-conducted speech analysis and robust communication systems for real-world applications.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The authors state they deliberately recruited a diverse and gender-balanced participant group to improve representativeness and inclusivity.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset required post-processing exclusions, and some issues such as inadequate acoustic sealing for certain ear canal anatomies were not always detected by filters. The speech-noisy subset primarily serves testing purposes because it lacks a clean reference.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing for speech enhancement, speech-to-phonemes recognition, and speaker verification; also potential use for voice commands, heart-rate monitoring, and synthetic data generation with realistic physiological and sensor noise.

name.evidence: Abstract —Vibravox is a dataset compliant with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) containing audio recordings using five different body-conduction audio sensors

description.evidence: Abstract —Vibravox is a dataset compliant with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) containing audio recordings using five different body-conduction audio sensors: two in-ear microphones, two bone conduction vibration pickups, and a laryngophone. The dataset also includes audio data from an airbome microphone used as a reference. The Vibravox corpus contains 45 hours per sensor of speech samples and physiological sounds recorded by 188 participants under different acoustic conditions imposed by a high order ambisonics 3D spatializer. Annotations about the recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions are also included in the corpus.

inLanguage.evidence: The Vibravox dataset was recorded in a 3D sound spatializer to sample uniformly the sphere for noise emission. Its unique combination of simultaneous multi-microphone recordings and French-language data therefore provides complementary resources to existing datasets

isLiveDataset.evidence: This highly curated dataset, comprising four subsets — speech-clean , speech-noisy , speechless-clean , and speechless-noisy — is now publicly available.

rai:dataCollectionMissingData.evidence: Mispronounced sentences, sensors shifting from their initial positions, occasional sensor malfunctions, or instances where a microphone was inadvertently left unequipped led to some data inconsistencies. Out of 200 participants, 188 were retained, with a total of 28,471 sentences.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: The Zoom F8n records all six sensor signals simultaneously, operates at a sampling rate of 48 kHz and a resolution of 32 bits, thereby guaranteeing precise signal capture with high fidelity. The text utilized for participant readings originates from the French Wikipedia subset of Common V oice [62]. A significant proportion of the noise excerpts were sourced from the Audio Set [66]. In addition, in-house recordings of concerts and street events in 3rdand 5th order ambisonics were also rendered around the participants.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: This textual data was further filtered to produce a simplified dataset with a minimum number of textual and phonemic symbols and to minimize pronunciation uncertainty. Once the unwanted sentences were removed, we applied common text normalization operations, such as lowercasing text and removing punctuation except for apostrophes. To enhance audio data quality, a 20 Hz high-pass filter is uniformly applied to each acquisition channel, effectively attenuating low-frequency noise and artifacts. we applied a series of three automatic filters to remove utterances with obvious deficiencies. The dataset is then split by speaker, with 80% of male and female speakers in the training set, 10% in the development/validation set, and 10% in the test set. Instead, the timestamps generated by V oice Activity Detection (V AD) are extended by 0.6 seconds on both sides. In rare cases where the adjusted start or end timestamps exceed the original audio boundaries, the audio is trimmed by 15 ms on the affected side.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: Annotations about the recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions are also included in the corpus. From this normalized text, we also generated the corresponding phonetic transcription using the Intemational Phonetic Alphabet (IPA), which contains 33 phonemes in French. This operation was done with the text phonemizer of the CoML lab [63]. A phase of manual phonetic transcription was then necessary for these unrecognized words, such as ” algorithme ”.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: The first filter discards any audio samples where PER[ j]>10%. This addresses potential discrepancies between the labeled transcription and actual pronunciation, ensuring high-quality labels for the speech-to-phonemes task.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: This operation was done with the text phonemizer of the CoML lab [63]. The whispertimestamped model3constitutes a key component of our indicator extraction process. This model is a speech-to-text engine based on Whisper [29] that applies dynamic time warping [67] to cross-attention weights.

rai:personalSensitiveInformation.evidence: The dataset is then split by speaker, with 80% of male and female speakers in the training set, 10% in the development/validation set, and 10% in the test set.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: We hope this release will drive progress in body-conducted speech analysis and support the development of robust communication systems for real-world applications.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Finally, to increase the representativeness and inclusivity of the dataset, a deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group of participants.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: However, in some cases, such as when a participant’s ear canal was too small for the rigid in-ear microphone to achieve proper acoustic sealing, these filters were not triggered. The speech-noisy subset is of particular interest for showcasing the noise-resilient capabilities of BCMs. However, this subset primarily serves testing purposes, as it lacks a clean reference under such conditions.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We conducted a series of experiments on various speech-related tasks, including speech recognition, speech enhancement, and speaker verification. The dataset is then split by speaker, with 80% of male and female speakers in the training set, 10% in the development/validation set, and 10% in the test set. These samples can be valuable for tasks such as heart rate tracking or simply analyzing the noise properties of the various sensors. It could also be conveniently used to generate synthetic datasets with realistic physiological (and sensor-inherent) noise captured by body-conduction audio sensors.
